mainTopic: The proof needed to uphold a contested document: רבי יוחנן and ריש לקיש on witnesses versus קיום השטר, and whether a document its writer admits to needs ratification.
overview: Our משנה is about a gift document: the heirs say the giver was a dying man (שכיב מרע), and the חכמים say whoever wants to take from the other must bring proof. רבי יוחנן says that proof means witnesses, while ריש לקיש says it means ratifying the document (קיום השטר). רבי יוחנן challenges ריש לקיש from the story of רבי עקיבא in בני ברק, where people asked to examine a dead seller's body. ריש לקיש answers that the buyers held the land and the family was the side challenging the sale. A support for this from the people's silence is brought and then rejected. Next, a teaching from בר קפרא leads to the question of whether a document its writer admits to needs ratification. רבי יוחנן says everyone agrees it does not, and he defends this against several challenges, including one from his own words to his teacher רבי ינאי. The גמרא settles this by reversing the opinions in the משנה, the ברייתא, and finally those of רבי יוחנן and ריש לקיש themselves. It then begins to explain why the earlier objection does not need to be reversed, and that explanation continues on the next amud.

steps.title: רבי יוחנן challenges ריש לקיש from the story of רבי עקיבא
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן argues that the ברייתא fits his view, where proof means witnesses. It does not fit ריש לקיש's view, where proof means ratifying the document, because then the buyers would have no reason to ask about examining the body.
steps.simpleTranslation: Granted, my view works: I say the proof comes through witnesses. רבי עקיבא told the buyers to bring witnesses, they could not find any, and so they came and asked whether they may examine the body. But according to you, who say the proof comes through ratifying the document, why would they need to examine the body? Let them ratify their document and keep the property!
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יוחנן uses the ברייתא of רבי עקיבא to attack ריש לקיש's view. He shows that the story only makes sense if the proof has to come from witnesses.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the story, the buyers asked whether they could dig up the body to check if the seller was an adult. That move makes sense if they needed witnesses and had none. If ratifying the document were enough, they could simply have done that and never needed to examine the body.

keyTerms.meaning: Granted / this works fine (for one view, before a 'but' about the other view)
Proof through witnesses (here, that the seller was an adult)
Ratifying the document, by confirming the signatures of the witnesses on it
To examine him (to check the body for signs of adulthood)

steps.confusionAlert: The text does not name the speaker, but this is רבי יוחנן speaking to ריש לקיש. 'לדידי' means 'according to me' (רבי יוחנן), and 'לדידך' means 'according to you' (ריש לקיש).

phrases.english: Granted, according to me,
phrases.notes: This is רבי יוחנן speaking to ריש לקיש.

phrases.english: since I say the proof is through witnesses,
since he said to the buyers: "Bring witnesses,"
phrases.notes: 'He' is רבי עקיבא, from the story in the ברייתא.

phrases.english: and they did not find any,
that is why they came and said to him:
What is the law? May we examine him?
But according to you, who say:
the proof is through ratifying the document,
why do they need to examine him?
Let them ratify their document,
and be established as owners of the property!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the earlier argument between רבי יוחנן and ריש לקיש about the משנה, now tested against the ברייתא of רבי עקיבא.
steps.kashyaTarget: ריש לקיש's view that the proof required is קיום השטר.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If ratifying the document were enough proof, the buyers in the ברייתא would never have needed to ask about examining the body. Their question shows they needed witnesses.

steps.title: ריש לקיש answers that the buyers held the land and the family was the challenger
steps.stepSummary: ריש לקיש says the challenge assumes the family held the land and the buyers were trying to take it. In fact the buyers held the land and the family was the side challenging, so the family was the one who needed proof and asked about examining the body.
steps.simpleTranslation: Do you think the property was held by the family, and the buyers came to challenge them? No. The property was held by the buyers, and the family came to challenge them!
steps.whatsHappening: ריש לקיש defends his view by changing the picture of the story. The buyers already held the land, so the family was the side that needed proof.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the buyers are in possession, they do not need to prove anything. The family, who wants to take the land back, must prove the seller was a minor. The family cannot prove that by ratifying the buyers' document, since they are attacking it. So they needed witnesses or a check of the body, and that explains the question about examining him without hurting ריש לקיש's view.

keyTerms.meaning: Do you think...? (introduces a wrong assumption the speaker is about to correct)
In the possession of / presumed to belong to
The family members (the seller's relatives and heirs)

steps.whyThisMatters: It shows a basic rule of proof: the side challenging whoever holds the property is the side that must bring proof. Who is holding the property changes who asked about the body.

phrases.aramaic: מִי סָבְרַתְּ נִכְסֵי בְּחֶזְקַת בְּנֵי מִשְׁפָּחָה קָיְימִי –
phrases.english: Do you think the property stood in the possession of the family members,
phrases.notes: Now ריש לקיש is answering רבי יוחנן.

phrases.english: and the buyers came and challenged them?
No, the property stood in the possession of the buyers,

phrases.aramaic: וְקָא אָתוּ בְּנֵי מִשְׁפָּחָה וְקָא מְעַרְעֲרִי!
phrases.english: and the family members came and challenged them!

steps.triggerLanguage: מִי סָבְרַתְּ נִכְסֵי בְּחֶזְקַת בְּנֵי מִשְׁפָּחָה קָיְימִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers רבי יוחנן's challenge from Step 1.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Redefining the case: switches which side held the property and which side was challenging.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The family held the land and the buyers were trying to prove their right, so ratifying the document should have been enough for them.
steps.terutzMaskana: The buyers held the land. The family was challenging it, and they could not use the buyers' document, so they needed witnesses or a check of the body.

steps.title: Support for ריש לקיש from the people's silence
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings support for ריש לקיש's reading. When רבי עקיבא said 'you may not disgrace him,' the askers stayed quiet. That fits if the askers were the family, but buyers would have protested that they paid money.
steps.simpleTranslation: This also makes sense, because רבי עקיבא told them, 'You may not disgrace him,' and they were silent. If the challengers were the family, that is why they were silent. But if the challengers were the buyers, why were they silent? They should have said, 'We paid him money, so let him be disgraced!'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא supports ריש לקיש's picture of the case by pointing to another detail in the story: the askers went quiet after רבי עקיבא's answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Relatives would accept that they should not disgrace their own family member, so their silence is natural. Buyers have no such feeling. They would argue that their money gives them the right to check. The silence therefore suggests the askers were the family, as ריש לקיש said.

keyTerms.meaning: This also makes sense (introduces support for the view just given)
To disgrace him (by digging up and examining the body)

phrases.english: This also stands to reason,

phrases.aramaic: מִדְּקָאָמַר לְהוּ: אִי אַתֶּם רַשָּׁאִים לְנַוְּולוֹ,
phrases.english: since he said to them: You are not permitted to disgrace him,
and they were silent.

phrases.aramaic: אִי אָמְרַתְּ בִּשְׁלָמָא בְּנֵי מִשְׁפָּחָה קָא מְעַרְעֲרִי,
phrases.english: Granted, if you say the family members were challenging,
that is why they were silent.

phrases.aramaic: אֶלָּא אִי אָמְרַתְּ לָקוֹחוֹת קָא מְעַרְעֲרִי,
phrases.english: But if you say the buyers were challenging,
why were they silent?

phrases.aramaic: לֵימְרוּ לֵיהּ: אֲנַן זוּזֵי יָהֲבִינַן לֵיהּ,
phrases.english: Let them say to him: We gave him money,
so let him be disgraced, and disgraced again!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Strengthens ריש לקיש's answer in Step 2 with a second detail from the story.
steps.raayaObject: ריש לקיש's claim that the family members were the challengers, not the buyers.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The askers fell silent after רבי עקיבא said they may not disgrace the body. Relatives would accept that, but buyers would have protested.

steps.title: The silence proves nothing, because רבי עקיבא gave a second reason
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects the support. רבי עקיבא gave two reasons: you may not disgrace him, and even if buyers argued 'he took our money,' checking would not help, because the body's signs of adulthood can change after death. So even buyers would have had nothing to answer.
steps.simpleTranslation: If the proof is from that, it is not convincing. This is what he told them: First, you are not allowed to disgrace him. And besides, if you say, 'He took our money, so let him be disgraced,' signs of adulthood tend to change after death.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא knocks down the support from Step 3 by showing why even buyers would have stayed silent.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי עקיבא's second reason answers the buyers' argument ahead of time: examining the body would not prove anything, since the signs of adulthood can change after death. Their silence therefore does not show who the askers were. The support for ריש לקיש falls away, though his answer in Step 2 still stands.

keyTerms.meaning: It is not a proof / that point is not convincing
Signs (here, the physical signs of adulthood)

steps.whatToRemember: רבי יוחנן challenged ריש לקיש from the ברייתא of רבי עקיבא, and ריש לקיש answered that the buyers held the land and the family was challenging. The extra support from the people's silence was rejected, because רבי עקיבא also said examining the body proves nothing, since the signs change after death.
steps.confusionAlert: This rejection only cancels the extra support from Step 3. It does not overturn ריש לקיש's answer in Step 2. His view still survives רבי יוחנן's challenge; it just lacks this added proof.

phrases.english: If it is because of that, it is no proof;
this is what he was saying to them:
First, that you are not permitted to disgrace him.
And furthermore, if you say: He took the money,
so let him be disgraced, and disgraced again,
signs tend to change after death.
phrases.notes: He means the body's signs of adulthood, so digging him up would not prove his age anyway.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the support brought in Step 3.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Only the supporting proof from Step 3, not ריש לקיש's answer in Step 2.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The proof assumed buyers would have had a comeback. But רבי עקיבא's second reason, that the signs change after death, already answered it, so even buyers would have stayed silent.

steps.title: A new source: a deed that the protester denies ever writing
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings the teaching from the משנה of בר קפרא, which ריש לקיש asked רבי יוחנן about. In the first case, the protester says he never wrote the deed, so the deed must be ratified through its signatures.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: ריש לקיש asked רבי יוחנן about a teaching in the משנה of בר קפרא. A man had been eating the produce of a field as if it were his. Someone protested and said 'It is mine.' The man in the field showed a deed that said 'You sold it to me' or 'You gave it to me as a gift.' If the protester says 'I never knew of this document,' the deed must be ratified through its signatures.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a new source to shed light on the dispute between רבי יוחנן and ריש לקיש. This step quotes only the first case of that source.
steps.deeperAnalysis: When the protester completely denies the deed, the holder cannot just wave the paper. He must ratify it by confirming the witnesses' signatures. This first case sets the baseline before the trickier second case.

keyTerms.meaning: A collection of teachings by בר קפרא, outside our משנה
A protest or challenge to someone's ownership
The document is ratified (made valid in court) through its signatures

phrases.english: Come and hear:

phrases.aramaic: שָׁאַל רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן לָקִישׁ אֶת רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן,
phrases.english: Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish asked Rabbi Yochanan,
about this, which is taught in the Mishnah of bar Kappara:
Here is one who was continually eating from a field,
phrases.notes: "Eating" a field means enjoying its produce over time, the way an owner would.

phrases.english: with the presumption that it is his,
and someone raised a protest against him,
saying: "It is mine,"
and this one brought out his deed,
to say: "That you sold it to me"
or "that you gave it to me as a gift,"
if he said:
phrases.notes: "He" here is the protester, not the man holding the field.

phrases.english: "I never recognized this document"
then the document must be ratified through its signatures.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the earlier support for ריש לקיש was rejected, the גמרא brings a fresh source connected to the same debate.
steps.raayaObject: ריש לקיש's view that the proof required is ratifying the document. The story ends with רבי יוחנן himself saying 'אין ראיה אלא בקיום השטר' (step 14).
steps.raayaSupportSource: The משנה of בר קפרא, as asked by ריש לקיש to רבי יוחנן

steps.title: Second case: the protester admits the deed but calls it fake or unpaid
steps.stepSummary: The protester admits the deed exists but says it was only for show, or that he was never paid. We follow witnesses if there are any. If there are none, we follow the deed.
steps.simpleTranslation: If the protester says, 'This is a deed written only for show,' or 'This is a deed of trust: I sold it to you, but you never paid me,' then if there are witnesses, follow the witnesses. If not, follow the deed.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא continues quoting the same source with its second case. In this case the protester admits he wrote the deed but claims it means nothing.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here the protester admits the document, so the question is no longer whether it is real. Even so, his excuse is not believed on its own: without witnesses, the deed wins. This is the detail ריש לקיש will examine next.

keyTerms.meaning: A deed written only for show, so the holder would look wealthy
A deed of trust, handed over before payment was made

phrases.english: If he said:
"This is a document of appeasement"
phrases.notes: It was written just to make the holder look rich, never as a real sale.

phrases.english: or "a document of trust";
"that I sold to you,
and you did not give me the money"

phrases.aramaic: אִם יֵשׁ עֵדִים, הַלֵּךְ אַחַר עֵדִים;
phrases.english: if there are witnesses, follow the witnesses;
and if not, follow the document.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִם אָמַר: שְׁטַר פַּסִּים הוּא זֶה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the same source with its second case, where the protester admits the deed.
steps.raayaObject: How a document is treated when the writer admits it
steps.raayaSupportSource: The second clause of the משנה of בר קפרא

steps.title: Does this teaching follow only רבי מאיר?
steps.stepSummary: ריש לקיש asks whether the teaching follows רבי מאיר alone. רבי מאיר holds that a document its writer admits to does not need ratification, and the question is whether the רבנן disagree.
steps.simpleTranslation: Shall we say this teaching follows רבי מאיר, who says that when someone admits he wrote a document, it does not need to be ratified, and it does not follow the רבנן?
steps.whatsHappening: ריש לקיש asks רבי יוחנן whether this teaching follows only one side of a known argument.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the second case, the protester admitted writing the deed, and the deed was accepted with no ratification. That fits רבי מאיר, who says an admitted document needs no ratification. ריש לקיש wonders whether this means the רבנן disagree with the teaching.

keyTerms.meaning: Shall we say? (introduces a suggestion that a source follows one opinion)
One who admits that he wrote a document

phrases.english: Shall we say it follows Rabbi Meir,
who says:
one who admits about a document that he wrote it,
it does not need to be ratified;
phrases.notes: The holder of the document does not need to confirm the signatures in court.

phrases.english: and not the Rabbis?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Draws an inference from the second case: an admitted deed was accepted with no ratification.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether the משנה of בר קפרא follows only רבי מאיר and not the רבנן

steps.title: רבי יוחנן: everyone agrees an admitted document needs no ratification
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן answers no. Everyone, including the רבנן, agrees that a document its writer admits to does not need ratification.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: No. I say that everyone agrees: when someone admits he wrote a document, it does not need to be ratified.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יוחנן rejects the idea that the teaching follows only רבי מאיר. He says this rule is agreed by all.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יוחנן says this rule is not a debate between רבי מאיר and the רבנן. If everyone holds it, the teaching fits the רבנן as well.

phrases.english: He said to him: No;
for I say: everyone agrees,
one who admits about a document that he wrote it,
it does not need to be ratified.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: לָא; שֶׁאֲנִי אוֹמֵר: דִּבְרֵי הַכֹּל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers ריש לקיש's question by denying that there is any dispute on this rule.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The rule that an admitted document needs no ratification is agreed by everyone, so the teaching fits the רבנן too.

steps.title: But רבי מאיר and the חכמים do argue
steps.stepSummary: ריש לקיש challenges רבי יוחנן with a ברייתא. In it, רבי מאיר and the חכמים argue about whether witnesses are believed when they try to invalidate the document they signed.
steps.simpleTranslation: But they do argue! As we learned: they are not believed to invalidate it. These are the words of רבי מאיר. The חכמים say: they are believed!
steps.whatsHappening: ריש לקיש pushes back on רבי יוחנן's claim that everyone agrees. He quotes a ברייתא where רבי מאיר and the חכמים clearly disagree.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יוחנן said there is no dispute. This ברייתא shows רבי מאיר and the חכמים splitting over people who admit a document yet try to weaken it: רבי מאיר says they are not believed, and the חכמים say they are. So the claim that 'everyone agrees' looks wrong.

phrases.english: But they really do disagree!
As we learned:
they are not believed to invalidate it,
phrases.notes: "They" are witnesses who confirm their own signatures but then say they were unfit to sign.

phrases.english: these are the words of Rabbi Meir.
And the Sages say: They are believed!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רבי יוחנן's answer that everyone agrees.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי יוחנן's claim that everyone agrees an admitted document needs no ratification
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A ברייתא shows רבי מאיר and the חכמים disagreeing about people who admit a document but try to invalidate it. So there is a dispute after all.

steps.title: Witnesses may weaken a document, but the writer cannot
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן answers ריש לקיש. Even if the חכמים let witnesses weaken a document, the writer who admits to it has no such power.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: Even if witnesses are strong enough to weaken a document, is the writer himself able to do that?!
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יוחנן answers the challenge from the ברייתא about witnesses. He says that ברייתא is about witnesses, not about the person who wrote the document.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא showed that the חכמים believe witnesses who weaken their own document. רבי יוחנן says witnesses have that special strength. The writer, though, has already admitted the document is real, so he cannot undo it, and no ratification is needed.

phrases.english: He said to him:
phrases.notes: רבי יוחנן is answering ריש לקיש.

phrases.english: If witnesses are strong
and can weaken the document,
is it in his power?!
phrases.notes: 'His' means the person who wrote the document and now admits to it.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִי עֵדִים אַלִּימֵי וּמַרְעִי שְׁטָרָא, אִיהוּ כָּל כְּמִינֵּיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא from the ברייתא in step 9.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinguishes witnesses from the writer himself
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The חכמים believe witnesses who weaken the document, so they must also require ratification when the writer admits to it.
steps.terutzMaskana: Witnesses have special power. A writer who admits to his document cannot weaken it.

steps.title: A statement in רבי יוחנן's name says the family protested correctly
steps.stepSummary: ריש לקיש quotes רבי יוחנן's own words: the family members were right to protest in the case of the document.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: But didn't they say in your name, 'The family members protested correctly'?
steps.whatsHappening: ריש לקיש challenges רבי יוחנן with a statement reported in רבי יוחנן's own name.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the בני ברק story in the ברייתא of רבי עקיבא, the family did not deny that the sale document was real, but they still protested. If they were right to protest, then even a document no one denies needs proof. That goes against what רבי יוחנן just said.

phrases.english: He said to him,
But didn't they say in your name:
The family members protested correctly!
phrases.notes: This is about the בני ברק story with רבי עקיבא from earlier, where the family challenged a sale made by their relative.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks רבי יוחנן's position using a statement in his own name.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי יוחנן's claim that everyone agrees an admitted document needs no ratification
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Saying the family protested correctly means the one holding the document had to prove it, even though it was admitted.

steps.title: רבי יוחנן denies saying it
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן says his student רבי אלעזר said that line, not him.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: אלעזר said that one. I never said this.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יוחנן pushes away the challenge. He says the quote was wrongly put in his name by his student.
steps.deeperAnalysis: He does not explain the statement. He simply denies it was his. So it cannot be used against his view.

phrases.english: He said to him:
That one — Elazar said it;
phrases.notes: Elazar is רבי אלעזר, רבי יוחנן's student.

phrases.english: I did not say
this thing ever.

steps.triggerLanguage: זוֹ – אֶלְעָזָר אֲמָרָהּ; אֲנִי לֹא אָמַרְתִּי דָּבָר זֶה מֵעוֹלָם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers ריש לקיש's challenge in step 11.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Denies that he said the quoted statement
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רבי יוחנן said the family protested correctly.
steps.terutzMaskana: That statement came from רבי אלעזר, not רבי יוחנן.

steps.title: רבי זירא: can he also deny what he told his teacher?
steps.stepSummary: רבי זירא asks: even if רבי יוחנן can deny his student's report, can he deny what he himself said to his teacher רבי ינאי?
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי זירא said: If רבי יוחנן can deny רבי אלעזר his student, can he deny רבי ינאי his teacher?
steps.whatsHappening: רבי זירא raises a new challenge. He is about to show a second place where רבי יוחנן seems to hold the opposite view.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A student's report can be wrong. A conversation רבי יוחנן had with his own teacher is much harder to deny. This step sets up the proof that comes next.

phrases.english: Rabbi Zeira said:
If Rabbi Yochanan will deny
Rabbi Elazar, his student,
will he deny Rabbi Yannai, his teacher?

steps.triggerLanguage: אִם יִכְפּוֹר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן בְּרַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר תַּלְמִידוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Goes around רבי יוחנן's denial by pointing to a stronger source.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי יוחנן's statement that everyone agrees (step 8)
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: There is another source, from רבי יוחנן himself and not from a student, that shows he held differently.

steps.title: רבי יוחנן told רבי ינאי the חכמים require ratification
steps.stepSummary: רבי ינאי taught in the name of רבי that an admitted document needs no ratification. רבי יוחנן answered that our משנה says the חכמים require proof, and that proof means ratification.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי ינאי said in the name of רבי: one who admits a document he wrote does not need to ratify it. רבי יוחנן said to him: My teacher, isn't this our משנה? The חכמים say: one who takes from his friend must bring proof. And the only proof is ratifying the document!
steps.whatsHappening: רבי זירא brings the story that backs up his challenge. In it, רבי יוחנן himself said the חכמים require ratification.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יוחנן read 'the proof is on him' in the משנה as meaning ratification of the document. So in his reading, the חכמים require ratification even for an admitted document. That clashes with his claim in step 8 that everyone agrees no ratification is needed.

keyTerms.meaning: one who admits he wrote the document
whoever wants to take money from another must bring proof

phrases.english: For Rabbi Yannai said in the name of Rebbi:
phrases.notes: 'רבי' on its own means רבי יהודה הנשיא.

phrases.english: One who admits a document that he wrote —
there is no need to ratify it.
And Rabbi Yochanan said to him:
My teacher, isn't this our משנה?
And the Sages say:
One who wants to take from his friend — the proof is on him.
The only proof is ratifying the document!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the evidence for רבי זירא's challenge in step 13.
steps.raayaObject: That רבי יוחנן held the חכמים require ratification of an admitted document
steps.raayaSupportSource: רבי יוחנן's own reply to רבי ינאי, reading our משנה

steps.title: רבי זירא: reverse the opinions, like רב יוסף
steps.stepSummary: רבי זירא accepts רב יוסף's teaching in the name of שמואל. The no-ratification teaching is the view of the חכמים, and רבי מאיר is the one who requires ratification.
steps.simpleTranslation: However, the words of our teacher רב יוסף seem right. He said in the name of רב יהודה, in the name of שמואל: This is the view of the חכמים. But רבי מאיר says that one who admits a document he wrote still needs to ratify it.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי זירא offers a way out. Switch who holds which view.
steps.deeperAnalysis: According to שמואל, the teaching that an admitted document needs no ratification belongs to the חכמים. רבי מאיר is the one who says it does need ratification. This fits רבי יוחנן's claim that the חכמים agree no ratification is needed.
steps.confusionAlert: Earlier (step 7), רבי מאיר was the one who said no ratification is needed. Here שמואל flips it: now the חכמים say no ratification, and רבי מאיר says it is needed.

phrases.english: However, the words of our teacher Yosef seem right —
for our teacher Yosef said
that Rav Yehuda said that Shmuel said:
This is the view of the Sages,
phrases.notes: 'This' is the teaching of בר קפרא from steps 5–6, that the admitted document needs no ratification.

phrases.english: but Rabbi Meir says:
one who admits a document he wrote,
it needs to be ratified.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the contradiction raised in steps 13–14.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רבי מאיר says no ratification is needed, and the חכמים require it.
steps.terutzMaskana: The חכמים say no ratification is needed, and רבי מאיר requires it.

steps.title: What 'everyone agrees' means
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן's phrase 'everyone agrees' means the majority view of the חכמים against רבי מאיר alone.
steps.simpleTranslation: And what does 'everyone agrees' mean? The view of the רבנן, compared to רבי מאיר alone, counts as everyone's view.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains how רבי יוחנן could say 'everyone agrees' if רבי מאיר still disagrees.
steps.deeperAnalysis: When the many חכמים hold one view and only רבי מאיר disagrees, the majority view can be called 'everyone's.' So רבי יוחנן's wording still works after the reversal.

phrases.english: And what does 'everyone agrees' mean?
The Rabbis' view, compared to Rabbi Meir —
counts as everyone's view.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes רבי זירא's answer by explaining רבי יוחנן's wording.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: 'Everyone agrees' means no one disagrees at all.
steps.terutzMaskana: It means the majority of the חכמים against a single opinion.

steps.title: But our משנה says the opposite
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא objects that our משנה has the חכמים saying the one who wants to collect must bring proof.
steps.simpleTranslation: But we learned the opposite: 'And the חכמים say: one who takes from his friend must bring proof!'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the reversal with the wording of our own משנה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the משנה, the חכמים require proof, which means ratification. That is the opposite of what שמואל's reversal says about the חכמים.

phrases.english: But we learned the opposite:
And the Sages say:
One who wants to take from his friend — the proof is on him!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the reversal from step 15.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The משנה clearly puts the requirement of proof in the mouth of the חכמים.

steps.title: Reverse the משנה too
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the opinions in the משנה should also be switched.
steps.simpleTranslation: Reverse it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers in one word: switch the names in the משנה as well.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the opinions are reversed, then רבי מאיר says 'the proof is on him,' and the חכמים do not require ratification. This keeps שמואל's approach consistent.

phrases.english: Reverse it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of step 17.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Switches the opinions in the משנה
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The חכמים in the משנה require proof.
steps.terutzMaskana: Switch the names, so רבי מאיר is the one requiring proof.

steps.title: But the ברייתא about witnesses also says the opposite
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings the ברייתא again: רבי מאיר says witnesses are not believed to invalidate the document, and the חכמים say they are.
steps.simpleTranslation: But it was taught: They are not believed to invalidate it; this is the view of רבי מאיר. And the חכמים say: They are believed!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא raises a second source against the reversal, the ברייתא from step 9.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The חכמים believe witnesses who weaken the document. That suggests the חכמים treat a document as needing ratification, which again goes against the reversal.

phrases.english: But it was taught:
They are not believed to invalidate it,
phrases.notes: 'They' are the witnesses who signed the document, the same ברייתא from step 9.

phrases.english: this is the view of Rabbi Meir.
And the Sages say: they are believed!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second challenge to the reversal, after the first one was answered.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ברייתא has the חכמים believing witnesses against the document, which matches requiring ratification.

steps.title: Reverse the ברייתא as well
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא again answers: switch the opinions in this ברייתא too.
steps.simpleTranslation: Reverse it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives the same one-word answer: switch the names in the ברייתא too.
steps.deeperAnalysis: With the reversal applied everywhere, the חכמים consistently hold that an admitted document needs no ratification, and רבי מאיר holds that it does. רבי יוחנן's statement that 'everyone agrees' stands.
steps.whatToRemember: Following שמואל, the opinions are switched in the משנה and the ברייתא. The חכמים hold that a document its writer admits to needs no ratification, and רבי מאיר disagrees. That is why רבי יוחנן could call it 'everyone's view.'

phrases.english: Reverse it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of step 19 the same way as step 18.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Switches the opinions in the ברייתא
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The חכמים believe witnesses who invalidate their document.
steps.terutzMaskana: Switch the names, so it is רבי מאיר who believes them.

steps.title: But רבי יוחנן said the proof is through witnesses
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא objects that רבי יוחנן's own words, 'proof through witnesses,' do not fit the switched version of the opinions.
steps.simpleTranslation: But רבי יוחנן said 'proof through witnesses'!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא points out a problem with all the switching it just did. רבי יוחנן's own stated view, that the proof must come through witnesses, now clashes with the new arrangement.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In their argument over our משנה, רבי יוחנן said the proof must come through witnesses. But in his reply to רבי ינאי (step 14), he said the only proof in that same משנה is ratifying the document. רבי יוחנן seems to contradict himself.

keyTerms.meaning: But surely! (an opening that introduces an objection)

phrases.english: But surely רבי יוחנן
said "proof is through witnesses"!
phrases.notes: He means witnesses who testify that the giver was healthy, not just people confirming the document.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the switching done in steps 18 and 20 by pointing to רבי יוחנן's own words.
steps.kashyaTarget: The switched arrangement of the opinions in the משנה and ברייתא
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: רבי יוחנן explicitly requires proof through witnesses, and this does not fit the side he now has to agree with after the switch.

steps.title: Switch the opinions of רבי יוחנן and ריש לקיש too
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the opinions of רבי יוחנן and ריש לקיש should also be switched.
steps.simpleTranslation: Switch them.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers with one word: switch. It now also switches what רבי יוחנן and ריש לקיש said.
steps.deeperAnalysis: After this switch, רבי יוחנן holds that confirming the document is enough proof, and ריש לקיש holds that witnesses are needed. That way, everyone's opinion lines up again with the switched משנה and ברייתא.

keyTerms.meaning: Confirming the document by verifying the witnesses' signatures

steps.confusionAlert: This is a third switch. First the משנה was switched, then the ברייתא, and now the two אמוראים, רבי יוחנן and ריש לקיש.

phrases.english: Reverse it.
phrases.notes: Switch what רבי יוחנן and ריש לקיש each said. Now רבי יוחנן says confirming the document is enough.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the objection of step 21.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רבי יוחנן requires witnesses, which clashes with the switched sources.
steps.terutzMaskana: רבי יוחנן holds that confirming the document is enough, and ריש לקיש requires witnesses.

steps.title: Should the objection be switched as well?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks whether the objection רבי יוחנן raised against ריש לקיש should now be switched too.
steps.simpleTranslation: Shall we say we should also switch the objection?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks a follow-up question. If the opinions are switched, should we also say that ריש לקיש was the one who challenged רבי יוחנן, and not the other way around?
steps.deeperAnalysis: Earlier, רבי יוחנן raised an objection against ריש לקיש. Once their opinions trade places, it might seem that the objection must trade places too. The גמרא checks whether that follows.

phrases.english: Shall we say we should also reverse the objection?
phrases.notes: He means the objection that רבי יוחנן raised against ריש לקיש earlier.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Follows from the switch in step 22 and asks what else must be switched.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether the earlier objection must also be switched now that the opinions are switched

steps.title: No, the objection does not need to be switched
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא begins its answer: no, the objection does not have to be switched.
steps.simpleTranslation: No.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts to answer with 'no.' This is a setup line, and the explanation of why comes right after it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The גמרא says the objection can stay the way it was, even though the opinions were switched. It is preparing to explain how the original objection still works.

phrases.english: No,

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Begins answering the question of step 23.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: No, the objection does not need to be switched. The explanation follows.
